British government ‘complacent about food as a national security matter’
article.full_text: Britain does not have a plan for how to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for potential future food shortages, according to a warning from more than 150 experts delivered to Andy Burnham. The climate crisis, geopolitical shocks, cyber-attacks and energy outages are among the threats to food chain security, according to the open letter, which claims the government is “complacent about food as a national security matter”. Academics, business leaders, community groups and food partnerships are urging the new government to treat food as a national security issue and work to make the UK’s food system more resilient, in a era when food supplies “can be weaponised”, they caution. The signatories warn that the “just-in-time” delivery system built up over recent decades “is not fit for today’s or tomorrow’s challenges”, as little stock is held along the food supply chain and the UK does not have any national food storage. Ministers wound up the strategic food stockpile that had been in place since the second world war in the 1990s. “The food system is exposed to shocks and threats from geopolitics, climate heating, ransomware, energy outages, software malfunction and disinformation,” according to the letter. The experts go on to warn: “These shocks will fall upon a system that is highly wasteful, import-dependent, environmentally unsustainable, and driven by the pursuit of private profit rather than resilience, with millions of people unable to afford a decent, healthy diet.” The letter calls on ministers to do the following. Establish a new system of local food resilience committees under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004. Audit the UK’s reliance on a few very large food companies and food imports. Realign national food production around nutritional needs. Create national, regional, local and community food storage schemes. Support the decentralisation of the UK’s food supply. The warning comes weeks after the National Audit Office, the public spending watchdog, issued a rebuke to ministers, accusing them of failing to do enough to help households and businesses plan for possible emergencies. The government’s own research has shown Britons are less prepared for potential future catastrophic events than citizens of several other European countries, while the UK is more reliant on food imports than some of its neighbours. The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, recently recommended that UK households build up stores of enough food and water to survive a few days without power or water, amid warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a wet, stormy winter to the UK. The letter claims the government is not paying enough attention to what such a store should look like, and is failing to consider that many lower-income households may not be able to afford to build up a stockpile. One of the signatories, Prof Tim Lang of the Centre for Food Policy, City St George’s, University of London, said: “We need a system shift: grow more food; more regionalism, diversity and storage at multiple levels, not just households; and public engagement in civil food defence. Central government must provide more strategic leadership while encouraging actions at different levels. Communities and households cannot resolve faultlines in the UK’s food system.” Prof Paul Behrens of the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, who also signed the letter, said: “Food resilience, healthy diet and environmental benefits all point in the same direction: grow more of the vegetables, fruit and pulses people actually need, closer to home.” The Cabinet Office is to launch a campaign telling households to stock up on tinned foods alongside preparations for future emergencies. The government’s Prepare website outlines steps it says people should take, which include assembling items at home that could include tinned meat, fruit or vegetables that do not need cooking. article.title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained
article.full_text: An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms. Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood. The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days. On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said. Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown. Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”. “My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?” The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing. Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday. The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts. More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff. The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war. The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human rights record, but has largely kept funds flowing. This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total, as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, according to a state department memo revealed by Reuters.
